source.title: Timer: Generative Pre-trained Transformers Are Large Time Series Models
source.authors: Yong Liu; Hao-Ran Zhang; Chenyu Li; Xiang-Dong Huang; Jian-Min Wang; Ming-Sheng Long

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text is garbled, but the relevant prose and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling evaluations to time-series models and reports downstream forecasting outcomes under changes in model and pretraining-data scale. It does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy or fit power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and reports downstream forecasting MSE as Timer’s model size and pretraining data scale increase, plus zero-shot MSEs for Timer checkpoints at different pretraining scales. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or small-run extrapolation. Table 16’s flattened layout does not support unambiguous assignment of all displayed values to scale conditions, so its individual values are not rowed.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream forecasting MSE as Timer parameter count and pretraining data increase, directly bearing on V6 in time series. It does not establish a power-law form, fit scaling exponents, or test quantitative extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that increasing Timer model size and UTSD scale improves average downstream PEMS forecasting, with smaller gains from data scaling. Their weak correlation statement concerns the broader zero-shot model comparison, while Appendix C.5 explicitly says scaling behavior is unclear on some datasets. These conclusions do not establish power-law scaling or quantitative predictability.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates time-series forecasting MSE across time-series models, model sizes, data scales, and zero-shot checkpoints; it does not use the language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law measurement or fit/extrapolation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcome varies by dataset and sample availability; zero-shot results vary across datasets and Timer pretraining scales.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 235, 2024
record.problems: The study reports downstream MSE rather than held-out pretraining loss and does not fit power laws or quantify uncertainty. Its zero-shot scale comparison varies pretraining corpora and does not isolate a single scaling variable. Table 16’s flattened layout prevents reliable assignment of its full set of individual numeric results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 16’s individual scale-sweep values were not extracted because the flattened table layout does not unambiguously associate every value with a model-size or data-size condition. The text’s explicit average model-size effects and data-scale trend are recorded in size-5, size-20, dim-5, dim-20, and data-scale.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling experiment.
No small-run power-law fitting or predictions tested on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation.
Architecture comparisons do not hold parameter count fixed; matching depth and dimension across backbones does not establish equal parameter counts.
Time-series scaling is studied, but whether its functional form is the same power law is not tested.
No quantitative predictive relationship, held-out scaling forecast, or mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance is tested.
No fitted exponent or compute-optimal split sensitivity analysis, and no test of departures from a fitted single power law.

missing.what: Moirai parameter-size comparisons from the study's own zero-shot evaluation. S/M/L have 14M/91M/311M parameters. MSE sequences are ETTh1 0.441/0.383/0.394; ETTh2 0.295/0.295/0.293; ETTm1 0.562/0.448/0.452; ETTm2 0.218/0.225/0.214; ECL 0.212/0.162/0.155; Traffic 0.616/0.425/0.399; Weather 0.195/0.197/0.221.

Combined model/data scaling endpoints: average PEMS MSE falls 0.231→0.138 with 5% samples and 0.194→0.123 with 20%, reported reductions of 40.3% and 36.6%. These are combined effects, not additional independent experiments.

record.verdict_notes: Timer-1B/16B/28B denote pretraining time-point counts. Their corpora are respectively UTSD, UTSD plus Buildings900K, and UTSD plus LOTSA; they are not a clean quantity-only scaling sweep. No uncertainty is reported for the scaling comparisons. Table 16's omitted individual results were already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fits or tests of predictions on much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token compute-optimal split.
No test of how depth, width, or architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count.
The study trains time-series models and examines downstream scaling, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.

Tests downstream forecasting MSE under Timer model-size and pretraining-scale changes, and across zero-shot Timer checkpoints. It does not test predictability from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling law.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal allocation, or comparison of fitting choices and curve shapes.

rows.value: The paper reports steady improvement with enlarged pretraining scale.
rows.note: Table 16 contains detailed results, but its flattened layout is ambiguous for assigning all values to conditions; this row records only the explicit textual result.
rows.check: The authors explicitly describe the benefit as relatively small compared with model scaling. Figure 11 reports average MSE approximately 0.148→0.138 with 5% samples and 0.129→0.123 with 20%. UTSD scale also changes pattern complexity and diversity; UTSD-12G uses a different shuffling strategy.
